headline: Brookfield Corporation: distributable earnings up 16% per share, $25 billion raised and buybacks near $900 million this year
takeaway: Distributable earnings rose 16% per share to $0.73, a cent above the consensus, and before realisations rose 14% to $0.64. Net income attributable to shareholders jumped to $1.3 billion from $219 million, Brookfield raised $25 billion of new capital, and the shares slipped 2.6% on the day.
results: Brookfield Corporation reported distributable earnings of $1,718 million, or $0.73 a share, for the third quarter, up from $1,487 million, or $0.63. Excluding gains from asset sales, distributable earnings before realisations were $1,496 million, or $0.64 a share, up 14%; over twelve months they reached a record $5.8 billion, or $2.47 a share.

Net income of the consolidated business was $1.9 billion against $284 million a year earlier, and net income attributable to Brookfield shareholders $1,305 million, or $0.54 a diluted share, against $219 million. Revenue was $20.7 billion against $18.9 billion.

The asset-management business raised $25 billion in the quarter, taking fee-bearing capital to $682 billion, and after the quarter received $13 billion of further commitments to its infrastructure flagship fund, bringing it to $26 billion. The insurance business originated $4 billion of annuity sales, and its portfolio yield rose to 5.7%.
mgmt: President Nick Goodman said Brookfield delivered strong financial results and that its focus on real assets with inflation-linked revenue, pricing power and durable cash flows positions it well for continued growth. He said demand for long-duration, essential-service and inflation-protected assets supported strong fundraising.

Brookfield repurchased more than $300 million of shares since its previous report, bringing buybacks to almost $900 million so far this year, reflecting management’s view that the shares trade below the value of the underlying businesses.
view: Brookfield Corporation is a holding company built around three engines: its majority stake in Brookfield Asset Management, one of the largest alternative managers in the world; a fast-growing insurance arm that invests annuity premiums in Brookfield’s own real assets; and direct stakes in infrastructure, renewable power, property and private-equity businesses. The quarter showed all three working, with the $13 billion infrastructure commitment after quarter-end a clear sign that institutions want exactly the inflation-linked assets Brookfield owns — data-centre power, pipelines, toll roads and utilities.

The jump in reported net income partly reflects asset revaluations and gains and should not be annualised, but distributable earnings growing in the mid-teens per share is the measure management asks investors to judge it on, and it is moving steadily in the right direction. The insurance business is becoming the most important driver: annuity sales of $4 billion a quarter provide long-term, low-cost capital that Brookfield can invest at higher yields in its own deals.

The persistent issue is complexity and the discount. Brookfield’s structure — listed affiliates, consolidated subsidiaries, insurance balance sheets — makes it hard to value, and management has argued for years that the shares trade well below intrinsic value, hence the buybacks. The insurance model also adds leverage and asset-liability risk that would show up in a credit downturn. For patient investors, steady per-share growth plus buybacks at a discount is an attractive combination; the catalyst for closing the gap remains simplification, which this quarter did not address.
watch: Watch fundraising for the infrastructure and private-equity flagships, insurance annuity growth and portfolio yield, monetisations that lift realised carried interest, and the pace of share buybacks.
